First, we multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity  $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}8\operatorname{sec}⁡5x(\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-{cos}^{2}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x & =8{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡5x\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡5x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =8{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡5x\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-\operatorname{cos}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=5x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=5x.$

| $x$ | $-\frac{\pi }{15}$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}8{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡5x\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-\operatorname{cos}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x & =8{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8}{5}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8}{5}(\operatorname{sec}⁡u-\operatorname{sin}⁡u){|}_{-\pi /3}^{0} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}(\operatorname{sec}⁡0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0)-\frac{8}{5}(\operatorname{sec}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{8}{5}(1-0)-\frac{8}{5}(2+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{5}-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{5}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
